ToolSpec: Accelerating Tool Calling via Schema-Aware and Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding

Heming Xia Affiliation:  Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Yongqi Li ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation:  Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Cunxiao Du Affiliation:  Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Mingbo Song Affiliation:  Peking University{he-ming.xia}@connect.polyu.hk; {harukioj}@outlook.com    Wenjie Li Affiliation:  Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract

Tool calling has greatly expanded the practical utility of large language models (LLMs) by enabling them to interact with external applications. As LLM capabilities advance, effective tool use increasingly involves multi-step, multi-turn interactions to solve complex tasks. However, the resulting growth in tool interactions incurs substantial latency, posing a key challenge for real-time LLM serving. Through empirical analysis, we find that tool-calling traces are highly structured, conform to constrained schemas, and often exhibit recurring invocation patterns. Motivated by this, we propose ToolSpec, a schema-aware, retrieval-augmented speculative decoding method for accelerating tool calling. ToolSpec exploits predefined tool schemas to generate accurate drafts, using a finite-state machine to alternate between deterministic schema token filling and speculative generation for variable fields. In addition, ToolSpec retrieves similar historical tool invocations and reuses them as drafts to further improve efficiency. ToolSpec presents a plug-and-play solution that can be seamlessly integrated into existing LLM workflows. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ToolSpec achieves up to a 4.2×4.2\times speedup, substantially outperforming existing training-free speculative decoding methods.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have substantially broadened their capabilities, including open-domain dialogue, mathematical reasoning, and program synthesis (OpenAI and others, 2024; Anthropic, 2024; Yang et al., 2025). In parallel, tool calling has emerged as a pivotal capability that enables LLMs to interact with external tools such as search engines (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025), calculators (Schick et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024b), and code interpreters (Gao et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024). By incorporating external tools, LLMs can alleviate fundamental limitations of standalone models, including outdated knowledge and arithmetic errors Qin et al. (2024a). As LLM capabilities continue to improve, tool use increasingly adopts multi-step, multi-turn, feedback-driven interaction loops to solve complex tasks Patil et al. (2024); Yao et al. (2025).

However, the growing frequency of tool invocations substantially increases inference latency, posing a major challenge for real-time LLM serving. Recent work has proposed several strategies to accelerate tool calling Kim et al. (2024); Zhu et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2024); Nichols et al. (2025). One line of research models tool-calling trajectories as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that capture inter-tool dependencies and then execute independent tools in parallel to reduce overall latency Kim et al. (2024); Zhu et al. (2025). Another line improves parallelism by overlapping tool execution with text generation, that is, launching tool calls while the model is still decoding, thereby further accelerating end-to-end tool-calling Xu et al. (2024); Nichols et al. (2025).

Despite these advances in accelerating tool execution, this work shifts focus to improving the efficiency of tool-calling generation. Our preliminary analysis indicates that generation latency can be a dominant bottleneck: on the widely used benchmark ToolBench Qin et al. (2024b), generating tool calls with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct accounts for approximately 80%80\% of the end-to-end inference latency and is roughly 4×4\times larger than the time spent executing the tools. Moreover, whereas tool execution time is often relatively stable for a fixed toolset and environment, tool-calling generation latency grows with model size and with the length of the generated tool-call sequence, making it the primary contributor to latency in many tool-using scenarios.

In this work, we present two key observations regarding tool calling: 1) tool-calling outputs are highly structured. These outputs are typically expressed in JSON and adhere to strictly constrained schemas. As a result, among the generated tokens, only a small subset corresponds to variable fields, while the rest are schema-determined; 2) LLMs exhibit recurring tool-call patterns across different requests, indicating the presence of reusable structural and semantic regularities. Motivated by these insights, we propose ToolSpec, a schema-aware and retrieval-augmented speculative decoding (SD) approach for accelerating tool calling. ToolSpec leverages the task-specific tool schemas to construct high-quality draft sequences, and employs a finite-state machine to alternate between deterministic schema token filling and speculative generation for variable fields. Furthermore, ToolSpec retrieves similar historical tool calls and reuses them as draft candidates, thereby further improving efficiency. Experiments on widely used tool-calling benchmarks, including API-Bank, ToolAlpaca, BFCLv2, and ToolBench, demonstrate that ToolSpec achieves up to a 4.2×4.2\times speedup and outperforms existing SD methods.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We propose ToolSpec, a schema-aware and retrieval-augmented SD approach for accelerating tool-calling generation. It presents a training-free solution that can be seamlessly integrated into existing LLM workflows.

  • •

    Extensive experiments across diverse models and tasks demonstrate that ToolSpec consistently achieves a 3.5×3.5\times∼\sim4.2×4.2\times speedup, with up to a 61%61\% relative improvement over the previous state-of-the-art SD method.

  • •

    Further analysis validates the effectiveness of our proposed components and highlights the impact of format adherence on ToolSpec ’s speedup, indicating its efficiency potential as LLM capabilities continue to advance.

2 Related Work

Efficient Tool Calling

As large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on multi-step, multi-turn tool-calling workflows, inference latency in LLM serving has grown substantially. To address this, recent studies leverage directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to model inter-tool dependencies, enabling parallel execution of independent API calls and thereby reducing latency Kim et al. (2024); Zhu et al. (2025). Another line of work executes tool calls proactively during generation to minimize system idle time (Xu et al., 2024; Nichols et al., 2025). In contrast to these prior methods that focus on tool execution, this work shifts attention to accelerate tool-calling generation, to further improve inference efficiency of tool-use LLMs.

Speculative Decoding

In recent years, Speculative Decoding (SD) has emerged as a widely adopted paradigm for accelerating LLM inference Leviathan et al. (2023); Xia et al. (2023). At each decoding step, SD first generates a sequence of draft tokens, which are subsequently verified in parallel by the target LLM (Xia et al., 2024). Recent advances in SD, such as the Eagle series (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025), introduce lightweight draft models layered on top of the target LLM, achieving promising speedups. While these approaches require additional training or parameters, an alternative line of research focuses on training-free SD methods (Luo et al., 2025; Saxena, 2023; Xia et al., 2025). Notably, Token Recycling (Luo et al., 2025) stores the top-kk candidate tokens of previous steps in an adjacency matrix and uses breadth-first search to construct a draft tree. Similarly, SAM-Decoding (Hu et al., 2025) leverages a suffix automaton to efficiently retrieve high-quality drafts from both the input context and a static text corpus.

3 Preliminary Study

In this section, we conduct an empirical analysis of tool-calling generation, covering (i) the latency breakdown between generation and tool execution, and (ii) analysis of tool-call patterns.

3.1 Latency Breakdown

We begin by analyzing the latency bottlenecks in tool calling. Experiments are conducted using Qwen2.5-Instruct series on ToolBench (Qin et al., 2024b). As shown in Figure 2, tool execution latency remains nearly constant across model scales, whereas tool-calling generation latency increases significantly, accounting for up to 𝟗𝟔%\bf{96\%} of the end-to-end latency for Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. These results indicate that tool-calling generation is the dominant bottleneck in tool-calling pipelines, particularly in multi-tool, multi-turn scenarios, underscoring the importance of accelerating generation.

3.2 Analysis of Tool-Call Patterns

Figure 3 shows an example tool-call trace from API-Bank (Li et al., 2023). As illustrated, tool-call traces are highly structured JSON objects that conform to a constrained schema, consisting of:

  • •

    schema tokens, e.g., ‘‘name’’, ‘‘parameters’’, and punctuation, which form the fixed scaffolding required by the tool-calling schema;

  • •

    tool and parameter names, highlighted in red and blue, respectively, which specify the target tool and its arguments;

  • •

    parameter values, in green, which instantiate the arguments with query-specific content.

These structured patterns distinguish tool-calling generation from general natural-language generation, suggesting that it can be formulated as a constrained decoding problem. In practice, valid tool calls must adhere to strict JSON schemas, implying that a large portion of the output tokens, i.e., schema tokens, is effectively predetermined. Once the target tool is selected, its parameter names are drawn from a finite, schema-defined set (e.g., ‘‘user_id’’, ‘‘time’’, and ‘‘health_data’’). Consequently, the model only needs to generate a small subset of tokens, i.e., the parameter values, conditioned on the user query and the dialogue context.

In the following, we further analyze practical tool-calling behaviors in LLMs, including schema adherence and recurring tool-invocation patterns.

Schema Adherence

As shown in Table 1, current tool-use LLMs exhibit strong adherence to tool-calling formats. Both the LLaMA-3.1-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Instruct model families achieve over 99%99\% accuracy in following the required tool-call schema. This observation further supports our earlier claim that tool-calling generation can be viewed as constrained decoding under a predefined schema. In light of this, acceleration methods designed for general text generation may be suboptimal for tool calling. Instead, explicitly leveraging the constrained-decoding structure can yield additional efficiency gains in tool-calling generation.

Repetitive Tool Calls

Beyond schema adherence, we observe that LLMs frequently invoke the same tools to satisfy recurring user intents and preference patterns. This behavior is consistently observed across widely used tool-calling benchmarks. As shown in Table 2, repeated invocations of identical tools occur frequently in API-Bank (Li et al., 2023), with the average number of calls per tool exceeding 10.9510.95. This observation motivates exploiting historical tool-call traces. Rather than discarding prior calls, a system can reuse previously issued tool calls when they remain valid, thereby further improving tool-calling efficiency.

4 ToolSpec

In this section, we introduce ToolSpec, a plug-and-play SD approach for accelerating tool-calling generation. The method leverages the highly structured nature of tool calls and recurring historical patterns to construct high-quality drafts with negligible overhead. As shown in Figure 5, ToolSpec integrates two complementary drafting strategies: schema-aware drafting and retrieval-augmented speculation, which we detail below.

4.1 Task Formulation

Given a user query and an input context containing system prompts and tool documentation, ToolSpec extracts tool specifications from the documentation and converts them into a structured schema. The schema defines (i) the set of schema tokens Σschema\Sigma_{\text{schema}}, (ii) a set of callable tools 𝒞tools\mathcal{C}_{\text{tools}} (e.g., ForgotPassword), and (iii) the parameter fields associated with each tool (e.g., Status, Username).

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote the target model, 𝒙\bm{x} the input context, and 𝒚=(y1,y2,…,yL)\bm{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{L}) the tool-call sequence to be generated. At decoding step tt, following the standard SD paradigm, ToolSpec first proposes a sequence of draft tokens 𝒚~t:t+γ−1=(y~t,y~t+1,…,y~t+γ−1)\tilde{\bm{y}}_{t:t+\gamma-1}=(\tilde{y}_{t},\tilde{y}_{t+1},\ldots,\tilde{y}_{t+\gamma-1}), as predictions of the subsequent decoding steps. The target model ℳ\mathcal{M} then verifies these drafted candidates in parallel and accepts the longest prefix that is consistent with its probability distribution. When the drafting process incurs significantly lower latency than verification, maximizing the acceptance length of 𝒚~\tilde{\bm{y}} directly improves the effective decoding parallelism and reduces the end-to-end latency.

4.2 Schema-aware Drafting

As discussed in Section 3.2, tool invocations from advanced LLMs adhere to predefined schema formats. This structural regularity enables deterministic drafting for large portions of the output. To exploit this property, ToolSpec constructs a finite-state machine (FSM) derived from the parsed tool schema. Formally, the FSM is defined as

ℱ=(𝒬,Σschema,δ,q0),\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{Q},\Sigma_{\text{schema}},\delta,q_{0}), (1)

where 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is the set of states, Σschema\Sigma_{\text{schema}} is the schema token alphabet, δ:𝒬×Σschema→𝒬\delta:\mathcal{Q}\times\Sigma_{\text{schema}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q} is the transition function, and q0∈𝒬q_{0}\in\mathcal{Q} is the initial state.

The state space 𝒬\mathcal{Q} decomposes the tool-calling generation process into structural components:

  • •

    qtq_{t}: tool-name state, where the model selects a tool from the predefined tool set 𝒞tools\mathcal{C}_{\text{tools}}.

  • •

    qpq_{p}: parameter-name state, where the model selects one parameter field of the chosen tool.

  • •

    qvq_{v}: parameter-value state, where the model generates the value of the selected parameter.

  • •

    qoq_{o}: “others” state, corresponding to general natural language generation outside tool calls.

As illustrated in Figure 4, once the special token <tool_call> is generated, the FSM transitions to the tool-name state qtq_{t}. In this state, drafting is executed via constrained decoding to generate candidate draft sequences. We formulate the proposed draft sequence 𝒚~\tilde{\bm{y}} as the concatenation (denoted by ⊕\oplus) of the necessary structural elements:

𝒚~=𝒚~prefix⊕𝒚~tool_name⊕𝒚~suffix\tilde{\bm{y}}=\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{prefix}}\oplus\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{tool\_name}}\oplus\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{suffix}} (2)

where 𝒚~prefix\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{prefix}} and 𝒚~suffix\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{suffix}} denote the corresponding schema prefix and suffix associated with qtq_{t}, and 𝒚~tool_name∈𝒞tools\tilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{tool\_name}}\in\mathcal{C}_{\text{tools}} represents the candidate tool names. All potential drafts are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Upon successful verification, the FSM transitions to the parameter-name state qpq_{p}, where ℳ\mathcal{M} verifies the candidate parameter names associated with the selected tool in parallel. The FSM then transitions to the parameter-value state qvq_{v}. Because parameter values are typically unconstrained, ToolSpec eschews schema constraints at this stage and instead relies on a general SD algorithm to predict these variable fields.

Then, the FSM transitions between states according to schema-specific delimiters. For example, the delimiter terminates the parameter-value state qvq_{v} and returns to qpq_{p} for the next parameter; while the delimiter marks completion of the tool call. Consequently, ToolSpec seamlessly alternates between deterministic schema token filling for structural states (e.g., qtq_{t} and qpq_{p}) and speculative generation for open-ended states (e.g., qvq_{v} and qoq_{o}).

4.3 Retrieval-augmented Speculation

While the schema defines the structural skeleton of a tool call and supports local drafting for constrained fields such as tool names, variable fields, particularly parameter values, depend heavily on the input context and cannot be inferred from the schema alone. Motivated by the recurring patterns in tool invocations, ToolSpec introduces a retrieval-augmented drafting strategy to accelerate tool-calling generation at the sequence level.

We maintain a datastore ℋ={(𝒉j,𝒚j)}j=1|ℋ|\mathcal{H}=\{(\bm{h}_{j},\bm{y}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{H}|} consisting of prior successful tool calls, where 𝒉j∈ℝd\bm{h}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the hidden representation of the input question 𝒙j\bm{x}_{j} at its final token, dd is the hidden dimension, and 𝒚j\bm{y}_{j} is the corresponding tool-call output. Given a query 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}, we retrieve the top-k most similar historical tool calls:

ℐk=Top−Kj∈{1​…​|ℋ|}⁡sim​(𝒉i,𝒉j)\mathcal{I}_{k}=\operatorname{Top-K}_{j\in\{1\ldots|\mathcal{H}|\}}\text{sim}(\bm{h}_{i},\bm{h}_{j}) (3)

where sim​(⋅)\text{sim}(\cdot) denotes cosine similarity and ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} the indices of the retrieved entries. Given the partially generated output 𝒚<t\bm{y}_{<t}, we align it with each retrieved tool call 𝒚′\bm{y}^{\prime} by matching the suffix:

𝒚t−L:t−1=𝒚′m−L:m−1\bm{y}_{t-L:t-1}=\bm{y}^{\prime}_{m-L:m-1} (4)

where LL denotes the suffix length and mm indicates the corresponding match position in 𝒚′\bm{y}^{\prime}. When a suffix match is found, ToolSpec extracts the next nn tokens 𝒚′m:m+n−1\bm{y}^{\prime}_{m:m+n-1}, using these continuations as drafts. As shown in Figure 5, if the current suffix matches a historical invocation containing , the subsequent tokens (e.g., ) are proposed as draft candidates. Intuitively, once the tool name and key–value pairs are aligned, the remaining structure of the tool call often follows recurring patterns, making 𝒚′m:m+n−1\bm{y}^{\prime}_{m:m+n-1} high-quality drafts for subsequent value spans.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Models and Datasets

We primarily evaluate our method using Qwen2.5-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) series, ToolLLaMA (Qin et al., 2024b) series, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). The evaluation covers four widely used tool-use benchmarks: API-Bank (Li et al., 2023), ToolAlpaca Tang et al. (2023), BFCLv2 Patil et al. (2025), and ToolBench Qin et al. (2024b). Additional details of these datasets are provided in the Appendix B.1.

Implementation Details

The retrieval parameter kk is set to 3. For suffix matching, we follow PLD (Saxena, 2023) and consider suffix lengths L∈{5,6,7}L\in\{5,6,7\}. The continuations are extracted using predefined lengths n∈{32,16,8,8}n\in\{32,16,8,8\}. We adopt Token Recycling (TR) (Luo et al., 2025) as the general speculative strategy in ToolSpec. Following prior work, we adopt speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2023) as our acceptance strategy, with a batch size of 1. Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix B.2.

Baselines

We primarily compare ToolSpec to three existing plug-and-play methods: PLD (Saxena, 2023), TR (Luo et al., 2025), and SAM-Decoding (SAMD) (Hu et al., 2025). For SAMD, we construct the static SAM from the input context and adopt TR as its decoding strategy. For comparison, we also include the advanced training-required method Eagle-2 (Li et al., 2024a) and Eagle-3 (Li et al., 2025) in our main results.

Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate ToolSpec using three widely adopted metrics: the mean number of accepted tokens (#MAT), throughput (tokens/s), and wall-clock speedup relative to vanilla autoregressive decoding. From a theoretical perspective, ToolSpec preserves the output distribution of the target LLM, thereby obviating the need for extensive evaluation of generation quality. Nevertheless, we report performance on API-Bank and ToolAlpaca in Appendix B.3 for reference.

5.2 Main Results

Table 3 compares the inference efficiency of ToolSpec with prior plug-and-play methods on widely used tool-use tasks. The results reveal the following key findings: (1) ToolSpec consistently outperforms existing approaches, achieving speedups of 3.5×3.5\times∼\sim4.2×4.2\times over standard autoregressive decoding across a range of models and tasks. Compared with the previous best method, it yields up to a 𝟔𝟏%\bf{61\%} relative improvement in speedup (from 2.5×2.5\times to 4.2×4.2\times). (2) The efficiency gains of ToolSpec are primarily attributed to a high number of accepted tokens (denoted as #MAT), ranging from 4.024.02 to 5.495.49 across different settings. Unlike model-based SD methods such as Eagle-3, ToolSpec does not require an additional drafting module and introduces only minimal drafting overhead (approximately 6%6\%, as shown in Figure 11). This low overhead enables the increased #MAT to translate more effectively into end-to-end speedup.

Discussion on Eagle Performance

We observe that the #MAT achieved by the Eagle series is lower than that of prior plug-and-play methods, such as TR, as shown in Table 3. We hypothesize that this gap arises because Eagle models are not trained on tool-calling formats, making such inputs out-of-distribution for these models. In contrast, as discussed in Section 3.2, tool-call traces exhibit structural regularities and recurring invocation patterns. These properties favor SD methods such as TR, which leverage historical traces to construct draft sequences. Building on this insight, ToolSpec exploits the schema-constrained nature of tool-calling tasks, enabling more accurate draft generation and achieving higher overall efficiency.

Results on ToolLLaMA

In addition to general-purpose LLMs, we further evaluate ToolSpec on two variants of ToolLLaMA, a model specifically trained for tool-use tasks. Figure 6 presents a comparison of inference efficiency between ToolSpec and prior plug-and-play SD methods on ToolBench. The results show that ToolSpec achieves a speedup of approximately 3.7×3.7\times over standard autoregressive decoding, demonstrating its effectiveness on specialized tool-use LLMs.

6 Analysis

This section presents a comprehensive analysis of ToolSpec. Specifically, we evaluate its effectiveness (§6.1), examine the impact of adherence to the tool-calling format (§6.2), and analyze the time allocation across different modules (§6.3).

6.1 Effectiveness of ToolSpec

Statistical Analysis

We first conduct a statistical evaluation to assess the effectiveness of the proposed modules, including: 1) Schema-aware Drafting. Figure 7 reports accepted token lengths in the first two decoding steps, corresponding to the tool-name state qtq_{t} and the first parameter-name state qpq_{p} in ToolSpec. As shown, schema-aware drafting enables ToolSpec to generate an average of 19.319.3 tokens across these steps. In contrast, prior approaches such as TR produce an average of 8.58.5 tokens, while Eagle-3 yields only 22 tokens on average, equivalent to standard autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the clear advantage of schema-aware drafting for tool-calling generation. 2) Retrieval-augmented Speculation. Figure 8 presents #MAT for repeated tool calls. The results indicate that ToolSpec consistently outperforms prior methods, achieving an average of 9.39.3 accepted tokens per decoding step and approximately 5.5×5.5\times speedup. This improvement highlights the effectiveness of the proposed retrieval strategy in handling repetitive tool invocations.

Acceptance Distribution

Figure 9 presents the distribution of accepted token lengths for ToolSpec in comparison with prior methods. While existing approaches typically yield accepted token lengths of fewer than 88 tokens, ToolSpec shifts the distribution toward longer accepted lengths, with 22%22\% of decoding steps exceeding 88 tokens. Furthermore, ToolSpec exhibits a pronounced long-tail distribution: nearly 4%4\% of decoding steps attain accepted token lengths between 1717 and 3333. This long-tail behavior stems from retrieval-augmented speculation, which reuses historical tool-call trajectories to produce longer and more accurate drafts. These consistently higher accepted token lengths contribute to the overall speedup achieved by ToolSpec.

Ablation Study

Table 4 illustrates an ablation study of ToolSpec and its proposed components. The results indicate that both schema-aware drafting and retrieval-augmented speculation are critical to the efficiency of ToolSpec. When these components are removed, similar to PLD, ToolSpec relies on suffix matching within the input context, resulting in slightly higher speedup than TR.

6.2 Impact of Format Adherence

Figure 10 presents the format adherence of different models in tool-calling generation. Adherence is defined by two criteria: 1) outputs must be correctly parsed as valid JSON; and 2) any extraneous natural language, Markdown fences, XML-like tags, or malformed JSON structures are treated as violations and penalized. The results reveal a strong positive correlation between format adherence and the speedup achieved by ToolSpec, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of approximately 0.900.90. Notably, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct achieves the highest adherence score of 0.9970.997, corresponding to a 4.45×4.45\times speedup on API-Bank.

6.3 Time Allocation

Figure 11 presents the time allocation across the primary latency-intensive components of ToolSpec. As shown, the decoding stage of the target model dominates overall latency, accounting for 91.0%91.0\% of the total runtime. In contrast, the additional operations introduced by ToolSpec, including top-kk retrieval and draft tree construction, incur only modest overhead, contributing just 5.7%5.7\% of the total latency. Despite this minimal overhead, ToolSpec achieves an approximately 4×4\times speedup in tool-calling generation, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing end-to-end latency.

7 Conclusion

This work presents ToolSpec, a schema-aware, retrieval-augmented speculative decoding approach for accelerating tool-calling generation. It requires no additional training or auxiliary models, enabling seamless integration into existing LLM workflows. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and tool-use benchmarks demonstrate that ToolSpec achieves a 3.5×3.5\times∼\sim4.2×4.2\times speedup while preserving output distributions. Further analysis highlights the effectiveness of the proposed components and the impact of format adherence on the efficiency of ToolSpec. We hope this work advances efficient tool use in LLMs and provides practical insights into scalable tool-calling generation.

Limitations

Due to computational constraints, our experiments do not include larger-scale language models such as Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024). Nevertheless, we expect ToolSpec to generalize well to these models and achieve further improvements in tool-calling generation efficiency. Additionally, our approach assumes strong adherence to predefined tool schemas and the existence of recurring invocation patterns, which are consistent with real-world application scenarios characterized by frequent tool usage. As discussed in Section 3 and 6.2, we anticipate that the effectiveness of ToolSpec will continue to improve as LLM capabilities advance.

Ethics Statement

The datasets used in our experiment are publicly released and labeled through interaction with humans in English. In this process, user privacy is protected, and no personal information is contained in the dataset. The scientific artifacts that we used are available for research with permissive licenses. And the use of these artifacts in this paper is consistent with their intended use. Therefore, we believe that our research work meets the ethics of ACL.

Appendix A Details of ToolSpec

In this section, we provide details of our proposed ToolSpec, including the implementation of parallel verification and the detailed algorithm.

A.1 Parallel Verification

Following prior work (Li et al., 2024b; Cai et al., 2024), ToolSpec adopts a tree-based attention mechanism to verify multiple candidate draft sequences in parallel. Specifically, the candidate drafts are compacted into a single flattened sequence and fed into the target model ℳ\mathcal{M}. The model then performs a single forward pass to verify all draft sequences simultaneously using a tree-structured attention mask, as illustrated in Figure 1.

To support different drafting strategies, ToolSpec employs two types of draft-tree architectures: (1) Static trees. For open-ended states (e.g., qvq_{v} and qoq_{o}), ToolSpec adopts a general SD strategy (e.g., TR) for text generation, where a pre-defined static tree architecture is used for drafting; (2) Dynamic trees. For structural states (e.g., qtq_{t} and qpq_{p}) and retrieval-augmented speculation, ToolSpec constructs dynamic tree masks that adapt to the length of each draft sequence, thereby reducing unnecessary verification computation.

A.2 Algorithm

We present the pseudo code of ToolSpec in Algorithm 1. Concretely, at each decoding step, ToolSpec checks whether the current suffix matches any sequence in historical calls. If a match is found, it extracts the corresponding continuations as high-quality drafts. Otherwise, ToolSpec employs a finite-state machine (FSM) to guide schema-aware drafting, thereby accelerating tool-call generation.

Appendix B Experimental Details

In this section, we present our experimental details, including dataset descriptions, implementation specifics, extended results, and additional analyses that complement our main findings.

B.1 Datasets

Our evaluation encompasses four widely used tool-use benchmarks. The details of the evaluation data are illustrated as follows:

  • •

    API-Bank (Li et al., 2023): A three-level evaluation framework comprising 73 diverse APIs. It evaluates an LLM’s ability to select and invoke tools through natural multi-turn dialogues across varying levels of difficulty.

  • •

    ToolAlpaca Tang et al. (2023): a benchmark for assessing general-purpose tool-use capabilities of LLMs. The evaluation dataset consists of two subsets: (i) a simulated subset with 10 synthetic tools, and (ii) a real-world subset with 11 APIs from diverse domains.

  • •

    BFCLv2 Patil et al. (2025): a comprehensive benchmark covering a wide range of scenarios, including single-step reasoning, multi-step tool use, real-time execution, etc. We evaluate ToolSpec under both single-function and multi-function settings.

  • •

    ToolBench Qin et al. (2024b): A large-scale, high-quality benchmark featuring multi-tool and multi-turn interactions over 16,464 real-world APIs, automatically constructed using ChatGPT. We evaluate ToolSpec on its single-tool subset.

B.2 Implementation Details

The retrieval parameter kk is set to 3, such that the top-3 candidates are retained at each retrieval step. For suffix matching, we follow PLD (Saxena, 2023) and consider suffix lengths L∈{5,6,7}L\in\{5,6,7\}, applying a longest-first strategy (from 77 to 55). Once a match is found, we extract continuations following the matched suffix in sequential order, using predefined lengths n∈{32,16,8,8}n\in\{32,16,8,8\} to construct draft candidates. We adopt Token Recycling (TR) (Luo et al., 2025) as the general speculative generation strategy in ToolSpec. All experiments were conducted using Pytorch 2.5.1 on 2×\timesNVIDIA A100-PCIE GPU (40GB) of 40 CPU cores under CUDA 12.4. Inference for our method and all baselines was performed using the Huggingface transformers package. Following prior work, we adopt speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2023) as our acceptance strategy, with a batch size of 1.

B.3 Performance Comparison

Table 5 illustrates the accuracy comparison between ToolSpec and vanilla autoregressive decoding across different models on API-Bank and ToolAlpaca. The results demonstrate that ToolSpec preserves the original performance of autoregressive decoding, achieving consistently comparable accuracy across various models and datasets. The slight discrepancy observed for Qwen2.5-14B on ToolAlpaca can be attributed to fp16 precision.
